chunks: As for what al-Husayn ibn Sa'id narrated from Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr from Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, he said:

I asked Abu 'Abd Allah (peace be upon him) about a woman who was with us on a journey, and she was performing the Maghrib salat — going and returning — as two rak'ahs. He said: There is no make-up upon her.

This does not contradict the first narration, because this is an anomalous (shadhdh) narration. And it is from the well-known, agreed-upon matters in which there is no doubt that the Maghrib salat during travel is not shortened (qasr), and that whoever shortens it is obligated to make it up. Therefore this narration is abandoned by consensus (ijma').

key_terms.بِالْإِجْمَاعِ: ijma' — unanimous scholarly consensus, here invoked to override the anomalous report
key_terms.تُقْصَرُ: qasr — the permitted shortening of four-rak'ah prayers during travel; Maghrib (three rak'ahs) is universally exempt from this
key_terms.شَاذٌّ: shadhdh — an anomalous narration that contradicts stronger or more widely transmitted evidence
key_terms.قَضَاءٌ: make-up prayer (qadha) — a compensatory salat performed when the original was missed or performed invalidly

ai.seo_question: Is the Maghrib prayer shortened during travel according to Shia jurisprudence, and what happens if someone shortens it?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi (in al-Istibsar) introduces a hadith via Muhammad ibn Ishaq ibn 'Ammar, in which Imam al-Sadiq (AS) appears to exempt a woman who prayed Maghrib as two rak'ahs during travel from any make-up obligation. Al-Tusi immediately reconciles the apparent contradiction with earlier rulings by classifying this narration as shadhdh (anomalous) and matruk (abandoned), invoking the established scholarly consensus that the three-rak'ah Maghrib salat is uniquely exempt from qasr (shortening) during travel — unlike Dhuhr, 'Asr, and 'Isha, which are reduced to two rak'ahs.
